key_idea: Order the cells so each has an earlier and a later neighbour: then every prefix and suffix is connected and the prefix stone count moves by at most 1, so some cut has exactly half. The pyramid has three leaves (top and two bottom corners), so one leaf must sit mid-order next to its neighbour and exactly one cut is invalid; a few different orderings dodge it.
sketch: Adjacency is the ordinary 4-neighbour one (the sample shows it). Odd stone count is impossible. Build five orderings: row sweep top-down ending in a bottom corner (and its mirror), column sweep from one corner to the other with the top leaf mid-order, and a 'staircase' order that runs down the left edge first and then sweeps columns (and its mirror). In each, take the first and last cut whose prefix has T/2 stones and accept one that a BFS confirms (both parts connected). An ordering can only fail if its mid leaf and that leaf's neighbour are both stones and the stones before them number exactly T/2-1; the row and staircase orders put different stone sets before that pair, so all five fail only in truly impossible cases (e.g. exactly the three leaves and their neighbours are stones, or the N=2 star). O(N^2). Any valid partition is accepted, so the checker's token compare fails on sample 1; my own exhaustive brute force (all stone sets for N<=4, 60k random for N=5, comparing existence and validating the output) confirmed correctness.
